category_title: Students who seek autonomy and independent mastery
minimal_context: Amir is sitting one-on-one with a tutor attempting to solve a Rubik's Cube.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Here is the Rubik's Cube. I will sit here and guide you every step of the way so you can solve it.

STUDENT: Okay. I'm just sittin' there trying to solve it. I'll keep trying and trying and trying.

TUTOR: You made a mistake. Let me tell you all these little things you could do to make it easier.

STUDENT: Every time I messed up I got a little more discouraged.

TUTOR: Just keep trying. I will keep sitting here and guiding you.

STUDENT: I gave up on it because I had like lost the little twinkle in my eye about finally solving the Rubik’s Cube and being able to brag to people. I never really started trying again cause I didn’t see the point.

options.A: Deliver verbal statements or gestures (e.g., high five, thumbs up) indicating approval beyond simple acknowledgment as he works on the Rubik's Cube.
options.B: Get the student started with the Rubik's Cube, step back to wait until he shows interest, and let him try to learn it on his own.
options.C: Point to an additional piece on the Rubik's Cube, sliding a finger out from the corner of the puzzle to guide his next move.
options.D: Point out specific patterns on the Rubik's Cube, identify more of the colors, and provide explicit explanations of the algorithms within the puzzle.
